methodological_rigor.justification: This population-based cohort study uses SEER-21 data covering approximately 41.9% of the US population and includes more than 1 million invasive cancer diagnoses from 2020 and 2021 with explicit exclusion criteria. The design is appropriate for estimating short-term survival changes during the pandemic, and the analysis stratifies by stage to address shifts in diagnosis mix. Statistical methods are generally strong, using actuarial 1-year cause-specific survival, 2015-2019 proportional-hazards trend models, expected survival estimates, absolute survival differences with confidence intervals, and mortality difference calculations. Limitations include potential within-stage severity differences, cause-of-death misclassification, unavailable COVID infection history, and residual confounding inherent to observational pandemic-era comparisons.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual population-based cohort study, so the Oxford level of evidence is 2b. The clinical relevance is high because it evaluates cancer-specific survival and excess cancer-related deaths during the first two pandemic years across a large US registry population. The endpoint is patient relevant, and the estimate of 17,390 additional cancer-related deaths within 1 year has direct implications for cancer screening, diagnosis, treatment capacity, and health-system resilience. It is not practice-changing at the individual treatment level because the exposure is an era-level disruption rather than a modifiable intervention tested prospectively.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is appropriate and is explicitly stated in the methods for this observational cohort study. The manuscript reports data source, population coverage, inclusion and exclusion criteria, subgroup definitions, stage definitions, outcome definition, statistical software, trend-modeling approach, and sensitivity considerations around cause-specific versus relative survival. Reporting would be stronger with fuller details on missingness, patient-flow accounting, and more explicit access instructions for all derived analytic code. Data availability is moderate because SEER is a recognized public registry source and software tools are named, but the normalized manuscript does not indicate that the authors deposited code or derived datasets.

novelty_literature.justification: The study addresses a credible gap: prior pandemic cancer research had focused largely on screening and diagnosis disruptions, while this manuscript evaluates 1-year cancer-specific survival for 2020 and 2021. The novelty is mainly empirical and population-level, using newly available registry follow-up to quantify survival decrements and excess deaths across stage, subgroup, and cancer-site strata. The conceptual framework that pandemic disruptions worsened cancer outcomes is already established in the literature the authors cite. The work is therefore a meaningful extension rather than a new mechanism, method, or paradigm.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is readable and logically organized, with methods that clearly define SEER-21, stage groupings, cancer-site categories, cause-specific survival, expected survival modeling, and mortality difference calculations. The abstract is self-contained and quantitatively reports the main survival reductions and excess-death estimate. The discussion appropriately connects findings to screening, diagnosis, treatment delays, and health-system preparedness while listing important limitations. Figure captions are understandable, though the results section contains some dense numeric reporting and at least one apparent typographic inconsistency in late-stage 2020 confidence limits.

key_strengths: Very large population-based SEER-21 cohort with more than 1 million cancer diagnoses during 2020 and 2021.
Clinically meaningful endpoint of 1-year cause-specific survival with estimated excess cancer-related deaths.
Stage-stratified trend modeling helps separate survival changes from pandemic-related shifts in stage distribution.
Discussion transparently addresses cause-of-death misclassification, within-stage severity, reporting delays, and unavailable COVID infection history.
key_concerns: Observational era comparison cannot isolate which pandemic-related mechanisms caused the survival reductions.
Within-stage severity, treatment delays, frailty, and infection history are not directly measured.
Cause-specific survival depends on cause-of-death coding that may be less reliable during the pandemic.
Code and derived analysis materials are not described as openly available in the normalized manuscript.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a strong, policy-relevant population oncology analysis with robust registry scale and clinically important endpoints. It fits Tier 2 because the design is observational and the main contribution is empirical quantification rather than a trial or mechanistic advance.
